newsitem.title: FRANCE: Bulgaria says French ex-defence minister was spy.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria says French ex-defence minister was spy.

text.p: Bulgarian secret services told France four years ago that the late Socialist ex-defence minister Charles Hernu had been a communist agent early in his career, a French former spymaster said on Wednesday.
Jacques Fournet, then chief of DST counter-intelligence, told France 3 television he could not check the report but passed it on to then-president Francois Mitterrand, Hernu's political patron.
Mitterrand decided to classify the report as secret since Hernu, his defence minister in 1981-85, had died in 1990 and could not defend himself, Fournet said.
"The DST was not able to verify what was in this report...We can regard this file as somewhat suspicious," Fournet said.
The weekly L'Express earlier quoted secret files as showing that Hernu had spied for the Soviet Union and other communist countries in the 1950s and 1960s.
Biographer Jean Guisnel said Hernu was too junior to know anything worthwhile at the time. The files did not say if he kept working as an agent after he became defence minister.
Le Monde said that in 1993 British intellegence services had handed French authorities a list of 300 French foreign affairs officials alleged to have spied for East European countries.
There was no immediate official comment on the report.

L'Express said Hernu was recruited as a rising political star by a Bulgarian spy in Paris in 1953, and was paid by Bulgaria, Romania and the Soviet Union for at least a decade for supplying reports about French politics.
It compared the Hernu case to the espionage scandals of British spy Kim Philby and Germany's Gunther Guillaume.

In Sofia, Bulgarian diplomat Raiko Nikolov, who was alleged to have recruited Hernu, told Bulgarian state television in a telephone interview that "he indeed knew Mr Hernu, but only in the way in which a diplomat has social ties with many people."
Todor Boyadjiev, head of the Bulgarian Euro-Atlantic Intelligence Forum (BUAIF), said in an interview with Bulgarian state television on Wednesday he doubted the story.
"This is not very likely because in this profession friendship and money do not mix," he said.

"However after the reorganisation of these (intelligence) services, there were cases of literal treason, when state secrets were sold for pennies," added Boyadjiev, who was a senior Interior Ministry official until 1992.
The BUAIF is a local think-tank grouping former intelligence officers who had to resign after the fall of the Berlin Wall.
Hernu's cabinet colleague Jacques Delors, finance minister from 1981 to 1984, told Europe-1 radio: "I'm stunned, I knew nothing about this, like all the French people."

The Socialist Party, in which Hernu was a key figure, cast doubt on the report and said all that mattered was whether Hernu had been "an intransigent protagonist for national independence, European and French security; the answer is yes."
Former spy barons also urged authorities to shed light on what if anything Hernu allegedly supplied his communist patrons.

"I've no idea whether this is true or false. Hernu was anti-Soviet and anti-communist, but on questions (of spying) there is a complete break between public and private life," Pierre Marion, former head of the DGSE secret service, which answers to the Defence Ministry, told Reuters.
"These accusations are too serious not to be cleared up."
Patrice Hernu, one of the late minister's sons, branded the report "a fabrication coarsely sown together" and urged President Jacques Chirac to shed light on the affair.
